translation_updates.summary: Being and Time (German: Sein und Zeit) is the 1927 magnum opus of the German philosopher Martin Heidegger. In it Heidegger pursued the question of being — the question of the meaning or sense of being — by means of a phenomenological exploration of the way that time structures our engagement with the world, introducing the concept of Dasein ("being-there") to describe the distinctive character of human existence. Human beings, he argued, must be understood as beings-in-the-world, and thus as constituted by our relationships to the practical and social contexts that give meaning to our actions; his analytic of Dasein underpinned his critique of post-Cartesian accounts of human beings as subjects in an objective world. The book, along with his many essays and lectures, profoundly influenced subsequent movements in European philosophy, and had a notable impact on literary theory and many other fields.

Being and Nothingness: An Essay on Phenomenological Ontology (French: L'Être et le néant : Essai d'ontologie phénoménologique) is a 1943 book by the philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre and his most influential philosophical work, in which he develops a philosophical account in support of his existentialism, dealing with topics such as consciousness, perception, self-deception, the existence of "nothingness", and the question of free will. A phenomenological investigation into the nature of what it is to be human, it defines two types of being: the in-itself (en-soi), the being of the object of consciousness, and the for-itself (pour-soi), the being of consciousness itself. The structure and characteristics of the for-itself are its main focal point, and it is there that Sartre gives his account of freedom and of the project of "bad faith," in which one's own real nature as for-itself is discarded to adopt that of the in-itself. Its 1943 publication has been described as "the groundwork of the Existentialist movement in France," and it remains, alongside works by Simone de Beauvoir from the same period, the defining treatise of the existentialist movement.

Micrographia: or Some Physiological Descriptions of Minute Bodies Made by Magnifying Glasses. With Observations and Inquiries Thereupon is a book by Robert Hooke about his observations through various lenses, published in January 1665 as the first major publication of the Royal Society. It was the first book to include illustrations of insects and plants as seen through microscopes, and it became the first scientific best-seller, inspiring a wide public interest in the new science of microscopy. In it Hooke first used the word "cell" to name the microscopic honeycomb cavities in cork, originating the biological term. Although the book is best known for demonstrating the power of the microscope, Micrographia also describes distant planetary bodies, the wave theory of light, the organic origin of fossils, and other philosophical and scientific interests of its author.

Either/Or (Danish: Enten – Eller) is a work in two volumes by the Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard, published on 20 February 1843 under the pseudonymous editorship of Victor Eremita (Latin for "victorious hermit"). Mostly written during Kierkegaard's stay in Berlin, it is the text he considered properly to begin his authorship, and is generally considered his magnum opus. The book outlines a theory of human existence, marked by the distinction between an essentially hedonistic, aesthetic mode of life and the ethical life, which is predicated upon commitment. Its first volume gathers the papers of a nameless young man known only as "A," who presents a view of what it means to live "aesthetically," while the ethical life view is set out in two long letters from Judge William, Kierkegaard's most famous spokesman for that way of living.

Process and Reality is a book by Alfred North Whitehead, published in 1929, in which the author propounds a philosophy of organism, also called process philosophy. It is a revision of the Gifford Lectures he delivered at the University of Edinburgh in 1927–28, and is his most comprehensive, if difficult to penetrate, metaphysical work. The cosmology it elaborates posits an ontology in which events are seen as networks (or "societies") of elementary and atomic events, called "actual occasions" or "actual entities." Whitehead's philosophical works, particularly Process and Reality, are regarded as the foundational texts of process philosophy.
